metadata.title: Comparing and Ordering Powers and Surds
metadata.description: Compare exact powers and radicals by common forms, safe monotonic transformations, and bounds before using approximations.
metadata.teachingApproach: Build rules from definitions, develop examples step by step, explain common misconceptions, and use exact checks. Each practice question has a targeted remedial explanation and a changed-value retry.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 9 “Surds and Indices,” printed pages 278–288. Approved scope: Compare positive fractional powers and radicals by converting to common bases or common root indices, using monotonicity only on nonnegative quantities, and bounding a root between nearby integers when exact simplification is unavailable. Explain how least common multiples of root indices produce an equivalent common-index comparison, and how raising both sides to a positive integer power preserves order for nonnegative values. Include sign/domain checks before applying these transformations, compare close values without premature rounding, and distinguish exact order from approximate decimal evidence. Draw examples from Chapter 9's surd comparison patterns; do not teach logarithmic comparison.

content.text: Welcome to Comparing and Ordering Powers and Surds. We will build each rule from its meaning, work through exact examples, and use practice to check both the method and its conditions.

Before comparing radicals, establish their signs. Squaring preserves order for nonnegative values, but not across arbitrary negative numbers. If both sides are nonnegative, a>b is equivalent to a^2>b^2.

A simple comparison often needs no decimal approximation. Since sqrt(7) and 2 are nonnegative, compare their squares: 7>4, therefore sqrt(7)>2. The check depends on knowing both sides are nonnegative.

For different root orders, convert to a common root index using the least common multiple. To compare cube-root(2) and fourth-root(3), use index 12: they equal twelfth-root(2^4) and twelfth-root(3^3). Because the twelfth-root function is increasing on nonnegative inputs, compare 16 and 27.

Do not compare only the radicands when the root orders differ. cube-root(100) versus fourth-root(90) cannot be settled by 100>90; the operation changes scale. Common-index conversion or a safe bound is needed.

Raising positive quantities to the same positive integer power preserves their order. If both values are nonnegative, square or take a common power to remove radicals; if they may be negative, first determine signs or choose another method.

For powers with common positive base greater than 1, a larger exponent gives a larger value. For a base strictly between 0 and 1, a larger exponent gives a smaller positive value. This reversal is why base conditions matter.
Example: compare 2^(3/2) and 3. Both are positive. Squaring gives 2^3=8 versus 9, so 2^(3/2)<3. Because squaring is increasing for nonnegative values, the comparison is preserved.
Bounds can avoid messy exact comparison. Since 4<7<9, taking nonnegative square roots gives 2<sqrt(7)<3. The endpoints are useful for eliminating choices or estimating an expression.

A sharper bound can be created by testing a rational candidate and squaring. To show sqrt(5)>11/5, compare 5 with 121/25; since 125/25>121/25, the inequality is true. Such a bound is exact, not a rounded guess.
Common-root comparison: compare sqrt(3) and cube-root(5). Use index 6: sqrt(3)=sixth-root(3^3)=sixth-root(27), and cube-root(5)=sixth-root(5^2)=sixth-root(25). Therefore sqrt(3)>cube-root(5).

For fractional powers, first ensure both expressions are real. A negative base with an even root is not real; an odd root may be negative. Taking an even power can erase sign information, so compare signs before raising both sides.
Approximate decimals can be a final check, but rounded values may hide a close ordering. Prefer an exact transformation when available and label approximations with ≈ rather than =.

Ordering several values works pairwise. Simplify exact powers, group expressions with the same base, and use bounds for leftovers. Do not chain inequalities unless every intermediate comparison is justified.
A quick direction check: for b>1, b^3>b^2; for 0<b<1, b^3<b^2. A mistaken monotonicity assumption can reverse an otherwise correct index comparison.
Use the practice to decide whether the quantities are both nonnegative, share a base, or need a common root index. State which property preserves the comparison before transforming.
A final answer should express the order clearly and preserve exact forms. If a decimal estimate is included, it supports intuition but should not replace an exact proof where one is easy.
